nodes.name: Roe's theorem
nodes.statement: Let $\{f_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}$ be a doubly infinite sequence of real-valued functions of a real variable with $\frac{d}{dx}f_{k}=f_{k+1}.$ In 1980, J. Roe \cite{R} proved that if there exists a constant $M>0$ such that $|f_{k}(x)|\leq M\text{ for all }n\text{ and }x$ then $f_{0}(x)=a\sin(x+\theta)$ for some $a,\theta\in\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.statement_short: A doubly infinite sequence of uniformly bounded functions with $f_k'=f_{k+1}$ forces $f_0=a\sin(x+\theta)$.
assumptions: Let $\{f_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}$ be a doubly infinite sequence of real-valued functions of a real variable with $\frac{d}{dx}f_{k}=f_{k+1}.$
there exists a constant $M>0$ such that $|f_{k}(x)|\leq M\text{ for all }n\text{ and }x$
conclusions: $f_{0}(x)=a\sin(x+\theta)$ for some $a,\theta\in\mathbb{R}$

nodes.name: Strichartz's theorem
nodes.statement: Let $\{f_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}$ be a doubly infinite sequence of functions in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ satisfying $\Delta_{\mathbb{R}^{n}} f_{k}=f_{k+1}$ for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $|f_{k}(x)|\leq M$ for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$, where $M$ is a real number. Then $\Delta_{\mathbb{R}^{n}} f_{0}=-f_{0}$.
nodes.statement_short: Uniformly bounded doubly infinite Laplacian chains on $\mathbb{R}^n$ force $f_0$ to be an eigenfunction with eigenvalue $-1$.
assumptions: Let $\{f_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}$ be a doubly infinite sequence of functions in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ satisfying $\Delta_{\mathbb{R}^{n}} f_{k}=f_{k+1}$ for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}$
$|f_{k}(x)|\leq M$ for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$, where $M$ is a real number
conclusions: $\Delta_{\mathbb{R}^{n}} f_{0}=-f_{0}$
nodes.label: th2

nodes.name: Homogeneous tree
nodes.statement: A homogeneous tree $\mathfrak{X}$ of degree $q+1$ is a connected graph with no loops such that every vertex is adjacent to $q+1$ other vertices.
differentia: every vertex is adjacent to $q+1$ other vertices

nodes.name: Degree assumption $q\geq 2$
nodes.statement: Henceforth we assume $q\geq 2$.

nodes.name: Distance on the tree
nodes.statement: The distance $d(x,y)$ between two vertices $x$ and $y$ defined as the number of edges joining $x$ and $y$.

nodes.name: Laplacian on a homogeneous tree
nodes.statement: The natural Laplace operator (or Laplacian) $\mathcal L$ on $\mathfrak X$ is defined by \begin{equation} \mathcal Lf(x)=f(x)-\frac{1}{q+1}\sum\limits_{y:d(x,y)=1}f(y).\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal L f(x)$ is $f(x)$ minus the average of $f$ over the $q+1$ neighbours of $x$.

nodes.name: Laplacian formula
nodes.statement: \mathcal Lf(x)=f(x)-\frac{1}{q+1}\sum\limits_{y:d(x,y)=1}f(y).
nodes.label: eq00

nodes.name: Eigenvalue function $\gamma$
nodes.statement: Consider the spherical function $\phi_z$ which is a radial eigenfunction of the Laplacian with eigenvalue $\gamma(z),$ where $\gamma$ is an analytic function defined by the formula \begin{equation} \gamma(z)=1-\frac{q^{1/2+iz}+q^{1/2-iz}}{q+1}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $\gamma(z)=1-(q^{1/2+iz}+q^{1/2-iz})/(q+1)$ is the eigenvalue of the spherical function $\phi_z$.

nodes.name: Counterexample to Strichartz's theorem on trees
nodes.statement: Note that the image of $S_1=\{z\in\mathbb C: |\Im z|\leq1/2\}$ under the map $\gamma$ is an elliptic region which intersects $\{w\in\mathbb{C}:|w|=1\}$ in infinitely many points. Assume $f_{k}(x)=\gamma(z_{1})^{k}\phi_{z_1}(x)+\gamma(z_{2})^{k}\phi_{z_2}(x)$ for some $z_1,z_2$ in $S_1$ such that $\gamma(z_1)\neq\gamma(z_2)$ and $|\gamma(z_1)|=|\gamma(z_2)|=1$. Since $\phi_z$ is uniformly bounded on $S_1$, $\{f_k\}$ satisfy all the hypothesis of the Theorem \ref{th2}, but $f_{0}$ fails to be an eigenfunction of $\mathcal{L}$.
nodes.statement_short: A sum of two spherical functions with distinct unimodular eigenvalues satisfies Strichartz's hypotheses on the tree but is not an eigenfunction.

nodes.name: Theorem A
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a measurable on $\mathfrak{X}$ and $z\in\mathbb R\setminus(\tau/2)\mathbb Z$. If there exists an $M>0$ such that $\|\mathcal{L}^{k}f\|_{L^{2,\infty}(\mathfrak{X})}\leq M|\gamma(z)|^{k}$ for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ then $\mathcal{L}f\equiv\gamma(z)f$. In particular, there exists $F\in L^{2}(\Omega)$ such that $f\equiv\mathcal{P}_{z}F$.
nodes.statement_short: Weak-$L^2$ bounds $\|\mathcal L^k f\|\le M|\gamma(z)|^k$ for all $k\in\mathbb Z$ with real $z$ force $f$ to be a $\gamma(z)$-eigenfunction, a Poisson transform of an $L^2$ boundary function.
assumptions: Let $f$ be a measurable on $\mathfrak{X}$ and $z\in\mathbb R\setminus(\tau/2)\mathbb Z$
there exists an $M>0$ such that $\|\mathcal{L}^{k}f\|_{L^{2,\infty}(\mathfrak{X})}\leq M|\gamma(z)|^{k}$ for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}$
conclusions: $\mathcal{L}f\equiv\gamma(z)f$
there exists $F\in L^{2}(\Omega)$ such that $f\equiv\mathcal{P}_{z}F$
nodes.label: Theorem A

nodes.name: Theorem A as an extension of Strichartz's theorem
nodes.statement: Since $\gamma(z)\in \mathbb R$ whenever $z\in\mathbb R\setminus(\tau/2)\mathbb Z$, Theorem A can be thought of as a suitable extension of Strichartz's result on homogeneous tree. In particular if we define $f_{k}=\gamma(z)^{-k}\mathcal{L}^{k}f$, then the statement of Theorem A resembles Theorem \ref{th2} with the only difference that the $L^{\infty}$ boundedness is being replaced by weak $L^{2}$ boundedness.

nodes.name: Theorem B
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a measurable on $\mathfrak{X}$ and $1<p<2$. \begin{enumerate} \item Suppose that $z=n\tau+i\delta_{p'}$ for some $n\in\mathbb{Z}$. If there exists an $M>0$ such that $\|\mathcal{L}^{k}f\|_{L^{p^{\prime},\infty}(\mathfrak{X})}\leq M|\gamma(z)|^{k}$ for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$ then $\mathcal{L}f\equiv\gamma(z)f$. \item Suppose that $z=(2n+1)\tau/2+i\delta_{p'}$ for some $n\in\mathbb{Z}$. If there exists an $M>0$ such that $\|\mathcal{L}^{-k}f\|_{L^{p^{\prime},\infty}(\mathfrak{X})}\leq M|\gamma(z)|^{-k}$ for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$ then $\mathcal{L}f\equiv\gamma(z)f$. \end{enumerate} In either of these cases, there exists $F\in L^{p^{\prime}}(\Omega)$ such that $f\equiv\mathcal{P}_{z}F$.
nodes.statement_short: For $1<p<2$ and $z$ on the boundary of $S_p$ at $n\tau$ (resp. $(2n+1)\tau/2$), weak $L^{p'}$ bounds on positive (resp. negative) powers of $\mathcal L$ force $f$ to be a $\gamma(z)$-eigenfunction.
assumptions: Let $f$ be a measurable on $\mathfrak{X}$ and $1<p<2$.
Suppose that $z=n\tau+i\delta_{p'}$ for some $n\in\mathbb{Z}$.
there exists an $M>0$ such that $\|\mathcal{L}^{k}f\|_{L^{p^{\prime},\infty}(\mathfrak{X})}\leq M|\gamma(z)|^{k}$ for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$
Suppose that $z=(2n+1)\tau/2+i\delta_{p'}$ for some $n\in\mathbb{Z}$.
there exists an $M>0$ such that $\|\mathcal{L}^{-k}f\|_{L^{p^{\prime},\infty}(\mathfrak{X})}\leq M|\gamma(z)|^{-k}$ for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$
conclusions: $\mathcal{L}f\equiv\gamma(z)f$
there exists $F\in L^{p^{\prime}}(\Omega)$ such that $f\equiv\mathcal{P}_{z}F$
nodes.label: Theorem B

nodes.name: Poisson representation of weak $L^p$ eigenfunctions
nodes.statement: It was proved in \cite{KR} that any weak $L^p$ eigenfunction of the Laplacian of $\mathfrak{X}$ can be represented by the Poisson transform of a $L^{p}$ function on the boundary.
assumptions: any weak $L^p$ eigenfunction of the Laplacian of $\mathfrak{X}$
conclusions: can be represented by the Poisson transform of a $L^{p}$ function on the boundary

nodes.name: Notation $\mathbb{Z}_{+}$
nodes.statement: The letters $\mathbb{Z}_{+},\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbb{C}$ will respectively denote the set of all non-negative integers, integers, real numbers and complex numbers.

nodes.name: Isometry group $G$ and stabilizer $K$
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be the group of isometries of the metric space $(\mathfrak X,d)$ and let $K$ be the stabilizer of $o$ in $G$.

nodes.name: Radial subspace $E(\mathfrak X)^\#$
nodes.statement: If $E(\mathfrak X)$ is a function space on $\mathfrak X$ we will denote by $E(\mathfrak X)^\#$ the radial functions in $E(\mathfrak X)$.

nodes.name: Infinite geodesic ray
nodes.statement: An infinite geodesic ray $\omega$ in $\mathfrak X$ is an one-sided sequence $\{\omega_{n}: n=0,1,2\ldots \}$ where $\omega_n$'s are in $\mathfrak X$.

nodes.name: Base point $o$
nodes.statement: Let $o$ be some arbitrarily fixed point in $\mathfrak X$.

nodes.name: Boundary $\Omega$ of the tree
nodes.statement: The boundary of $\mathfrak X$ is the set of all infinite geodesic rays starting at $o$ and will be denoted by $\Omega$.
nodes.genus: the set of all infinite geodesic rays

nodes.name: Boundary measure $\nu$
nodes.statement: Let $\nu$ be the $G$-quasi-invariant probability measure on the boundary $\Omega$.

nodes.name: Poisson kernel
nodes.statement: The Poisson kernel $p(g\cdot o,\omega)$ is the Radon-Nikodym derivative $d\nu(g^{-1}\omega)/d\nu(\omega)$ and explicitly written as $$ p(x,\omega)=q^{h_{\omega}(x)} \;\; \forall x\in \mathfrak X \;\; \forall \omega\in\Omega,$$ where $h_{\omega}(x)$ is the height of $x$ in $\mathfrak X$ with respect to $\omega$ (see \cite{FTC} for details).
nodes.statement_short: The Poisson kernel is $p(x,\omega)=q^{h_\omega(x)}$ with $h_\omega$ the horocyclic height.

nodes.name: Poisson transform $\mathcal{P}_z$
nodes.statement: The Poisson transformation $\mathcal{P}_{z}:C(\Omega)\rightarrow C(\mathfrak X)$ is given by the formula $$\mathcal{P}_{z}\eta(x)=\int\limits_{\Omega}p^{1/2+iz}(x,\omega)\eta(\omega)d\nu(\omega).$$
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal P_z\eta(x)=\int_\Omega p^{1/2+iz}(x,\omega)\eta(\omega)d\nu(\omega)$.

nodes.name: Period $\tau$
nodes.statement: It is obvious that $\mathcal{P}_{z}=\mathcal{P}_{z+\tau}$, where $\tau=2\pi/\log q$.

nodes.name: Poisson transforms are eigenfunctions of $\mathcal L$
nodes.statement: It is a well-known fact that $\mathcal L \mathcal{P}_{z}\eta(x) =\gamma(z) \mathcal{P}_{z}\eta(x)$ for every $z$ in $\mathbb{C},$ where expression of $\gamma(z)$ is given in (\ref{eq01}).
assumptions: for every $z$ in $\mathbb{C},$
conclusions: $\mathcal L \mathcal{P}_{z}\eta(x) =\gamma(z) \mathcal{P}_{z}\eta(x)$

nodes.name: Elementary spherical function $\phi_z$
nodes.statement: The elementary spherical function $\phi_z$ on $\mathfrak X$ is the Poisson transform of the constant function $\mathbf{1}$.

nodes.name: $\phi_z$ is the normalized radial eigenfunction
nodes.statement: Note that $\phi_z$ is the radial eigenfunction of $\mathcal L$ with eigenvalue $\gamma(z)$ such that $\phi_z(o)=1$.
conclusions: $\phi_z$ is the radial eigenfunction of $\mathcal L$ with eigenvalue $\gamma(z)$ such that $\phi_z(o)=1$

nodes.name: Radialization $\varepsilon f$
nodes.statement: For a suitable function $f$ on $\mathfrak{X}$, its radialization $\varepsilon f$ is defined as \begin{equation} \varepsilon f(x)=\int\limits_{K}f(k\cdot x)dk, \end{equation} where $dk$ is the normalized measure on $K$.

nodes.name: Radialization formula
nodes.statement: \varepsilon f(x)=\int\limits_{K}f(k\cdot x)dk,
nodes.label: Equation 2.3

nodes.name: Properties of radialization
nodes.statement: Some useful facts about radialization: \begin{enumerate} \item $\|\varepsilon f\|_{p,q}\leq\|f\|_{p,q}$ whenever $1<p<\infty$, $1\leq q\leq\infty$. \item The operator $\varepsilon$ commutes with the Laplacian $\mathcal{L}$, that is $\mathcal{L}(\varepsilon f)=\varepsilon(\mathcal{L}f).$ \item Also if $\mathcal L u=\gamma(z)u$ then $\varepsilon u (x)=u(o)\phi_z(x)$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Radialization is a Lorentz-norm contraction, commutes with $\mathcal L$, and maps a $\gamma(z)$-eigenfunction $u$ to $u(o)\phi_z$.
conclusions: $\|\varepsilon f\|_{p,q}\leq\|f\|_{p,q}$ whenever $1<p<\infty$, $1\leq q\leq\infty$.
The operator $\varepsilon$ commutes with the Laplacian $\mathcal{L}$, that is $\mathcal{L}(\varepsilon f)=\varepsilon(\mathcal{L}f).$
Also if $\mathcal L u=\gamma(z)u$ then $\varepsilon u (x)=u(o)\phi_z(x)$.

nodes.name: Explicit formula for the spherical function
nodes.statement: The following expression of the function $\phi_z$ is well-known (see \cite{FTP1}) \begin{equation} \phi_z(x)= \begin{cases} \vspace*{.2cm} \left(\frac{q-1}{q+1}|x|+1\right)q^{-|x|/2}&\forall z\in\ \tau\mathbb Z\\ \vspace*{.2cm}\left(\frac{q-1}{q+1}|x|+1\right)q^{-|x|/2}(-1)^{|x|}&\forall z\in {\tau/2}+\tau\mathbb Z\\ \mathbf{c}(z)q^{{(iz-1/2)}|x|}+\mathbf{c}(-z)q^{{(-iz-1/2)}|x|}&\forall z\in\mathbb C\setminus(\tau/2)\mathbb Z, \end{cases} \end{equation} where $\mathbf{c}$ is a meromorphic function given by $$\mathbf{c}(z)=\frac{q^{1/2}}{q+1}\frac{q^{1/2+iz}-q^{-{1/2}-iz}}{q^{iz}-q^{-iz}}\quad\forall z\in (\tau/2)\mathbb Z.$$
nodes.statement_short: Closed form of $\phi_z(x)$ in terms of $|x|$: polynomial-times-$q^{-|x|/2}$ on $(\tau/2)\mathbb Z$, otherwise a Harish-Chandra $\mathbf c$-function expansion.

nodes.name: Spherical function expansion
nodes.statement: \phi_z(x)= \begin{cases} \vspace*{.2cm} \left(\frac{q-1}{q+1}|x|+1\right)q^{-|x|/2}&\forall z\in\ \tau\mathbb Z\\ \vspace*{.2cm}\left(\frac{q-1}{q+1}|x|+1\right)q^{-|x|/2}(-1)^{|x|}&\forall z\in {\tau/2}+\tau\mathbb Z\\ \mathbf{c}(z)q^{{(iz-1/2)}|x|}+\mathbf{c}(-z)q^{{(-iz-1/2)}|x|}&\forall z\in\mathbb C\setminus(\tau/2)\mathbb Z, \end{cases}
nodes.label: eqsf

nodes.name: Spherical functions are bounded on $S_1$
nodes.statement: It is easy to verify that $|\phi_{z}(x)|\leq 1$ for all $x\in\mathfrak X$ whenever $z\in S_1=\{z\in\mathbb C: |\Im z|\leq1/2\}$.
assumptions: whenever $z\in S_1=\{z\in\mathbb C: |\Im z|\leq1/2\}$
conclusions: $|\phi_{z}(x)|\leq 1$ for all $x\in\mathfrak X$

nodes.name: $\delta_p$ and strip $S_p$
nodes.statement: For $p\in(1,\infty)$ we define $$\delta_p=\frac{1}{p}-\frac{1}{2}\;\;\; \text{and}\;\;\; S_p=\{z\in\mathbb C: |\Im z|\leq|\delta_p|\}.$$
nodes.statement_short: $\delta_p=1/p-1/2$ and $S_p$ is the strip $|\Im z|\le|\delta_p|$.

nodes.name: Convention $\delta_1=1/2$
nodes.statement: We assume $\delta_1=-\delta_\infty=1/2$ so that $S_1=\{z\in\mathbb C: |\Im z|\leq1/2\}$.

nodes.name: Interior and boundary of $S_p$
nodes.statement: We shall henceforth write $S_p^\circ$ and $\partial{S_p}$ to denote the usual interior and boundary of $S_p$ respectively.

nodes.name: Proof pointer for Lemma 2.1
nodes.statement: The following norm estimates of $\phi_{z}$ can be derived by using (\ref{eqsf}) (see \cite{FTP1} for details).
nodes.statement_short: Derived from the explicit formula for $\phi_z$; details in the cited reference.

nodes.name: Lorentz-space membership of spherical functions
nodes.statement: Let $1<p<2$. Then \begin{enumerate} \item[$1.$] $\phi_z\in L^{p'}(\mathfrak X)\quad\text{if and only if}\quad z\in S_p^\circ$ \item[$2.$] $\phi_z\in L^{p',\infty}(\mathfrak X)\quad\text{if and only if}\quad z\in S_p.$ \item[$3.$] $\phi_z\notin L^{2,\infty}(\mathfrak X)$ if $z\in(\tau/2)\mathbb Z$ and $\phi_z\in L^{2,\infty}(\mathfrak X)$ if $z\in\mathbb R\setminus(\tau/2)\mathbb Z$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: $\phi_z\in L^{p'}$ iff $z\in S_p^\circ$, $\phi_z\in L^{p',\infty}$ iff $z\in S_p$, and $\phi_z\in L^{2,\infty}$ iff $z$ real and not in $(\tau/2)\mathbb Z$.
conclusions: $\phi_z\in L^{p'}(\mathfrak X)\quad\text{if and only if}\quad z\in S_p^\circ$
$\phi_z\in L^{p',\infty}(\mathfrak X)\quad\text{if and only if}\quad z\in S_p.$
$\phi_z\notin L^{2,\infty}(\mathfrak X)$ if $z\in(\tau/2)\mathbb Z$ and $\phi_z\in L^{2,\infty}(\mathfrak X)$ if $z\in\mathbb R\setminus(\tau/2)\mathbb Z$.
nodes.label: phiz

nodes.name: $\gamma(S_p^\circ)$ lies in the point spectrum
nodes.statement: From the above lemma it is clear that $\gamma(S_p^\circ)$ lies in the point spectrum of the $\mathcal L,$ which is a bounded operator on $L^{p^\prime}(\mathfrak X)$.
conclusions: $\gamma(S_p^\circ)$ lies in the point spectrum of the $\mathcal L,$

nodes.name: $L^p$-spectrum of the Laplacian on a homogeneous tree
nodes.statement: For every $p\in[1,\infty]$, the $L^{p}$-spectrum $\sigma_{p}(\mathcal{L})$ of $\mathcal{L}$ is the image of $S_p$ under the map $\gamma$, which is precisely the set of all $w$ in $\mathbb{C}$ which satisfies \begin{equation} \left[\frac{1-\mbox{Re }(w)}{b\cosh(\delta_{p}\log q)}\right]^{2}+\left[\frac{\Im(w)}{b\sinh(\delta_{p}\log q)}\right]^{2}\leq 1,\text{ where }b=\frac{2\sqrt{q}}{q+1}. \end{equation} In particular, $\sigma_{2}(\mathcal{L})$ degenerates into the line segment $[1-b,1+b]$.
nodes.statement_short: The $L^p$-spectrum of $\mathcal L$ is $\gamma(S_p)$, a filled ellipse; for $p=2$ it is the segment $[1-b,1+b]$.
assumptions: For every $p\in[1,\infty]$
conclusions: the $L^{p}$-spectrum $\sigma_{p}(\mathcal{L})$ of $\mathcal{L}$ is the image of $S_p$ under the map $\gamma$
In particular, $\sigma_{2}(\mathcal{L})$ degenerates into the line segment $[1-b,1+b]$.

nodes.name: Elliptic region of the $L^p$-spectrum
nodes.statement: \left[\frac{1-\mbox{Re }(w)}{b\cosh(\delta_{p}\log q)}\right]^{2}+\left[\frac{\Im(w)}{b\sinh(\delta_{p}\log q)}\right]^{2}\leq 1,\text{ where }b=\frac{2\sqrt{q}}{q+1}.
nodes.label: equation 1.2

nodes.name: Spherical Fourier transform
nodes.statement: The spherical Fourier transform $\hat{f}$ of a finitely supported radial function $f$ is defined by \begin{equation} \hat{f}(z)=\sum\limits_{x\in\mathfrak X}f(x)\phi_z(x)\quad\text{ where }z\in\mathbb C. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Spherical Fourier transform formula
nodes.statement: \hat{f}(z)=\sum\limits_{x\in\mathfrak X}f(x)\phi_z(x)\quad\text{ where }z\in\mathbb C.
nodes.label: Equation 2.6

nodes.name: Spherical transforms are even and $\tau$-periodic
nodes.statement: The symmetric properties of the spherical function implies that $\hat{f}$ is even and $\tau$-periodic on $\mathbb{C}$.
conclusions: $\hat{f}$ is even and $\tau$-periodic on $\mathbb{C}$

nodes.name: $p$-Schwartz space $\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})$
nodes.statement: For $1<p\leq 2$, we define the space $\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})$ which consists of all those functions $f$ defined on $\mathfrak{X}$ such that \begin{equation} \nu_{m}(f)=\sup\limits_{x\in\mathfrak{X}}(1+|x|)^{m}q^{|x|/p}|f(x)|<\infty,\text{ for all }m\in\mathbb{N}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Functions with $(1+|x|)^m q^{|x|/p}|f(x)|$ bounded for every $m$.

nodes.name: Seminorms $\nu_m$
nodes.statement: \nu_{m}(f)=\sup\limits_{x\in\mathfrak{X}}(1+|x|)^{m}q^{|x|/p}|f(x)|<\infty,\text{ for all }m\in\mathbb{N}.
nodes.label: Equation 2.7

nodes.name: $\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})$ is a Fréchet space
nodes.statement: It is known that $\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})$ form Fr\'{e}chet space with respect to these countable seminorms $\nu_{m}(\cdot)$ and are also known as the $p$-Schwartz spaces of rapidly decreasing functions on $\mathfrak{X}$ (see \cite{CMS}).
conclusions: $\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})$ form Fr\'{e}chet space with respect to these countable seminorms $\nu_{m}(\cdot)$

nodes.name: Space $\mathcal{H}(S_{p})^{\#}$
nodes.statement: For $1<p\leq 2$, we also define the space $\mathcal{H}(S_{p})^{\#}$ of all even, $\tau$-periodic function $g$ on $S_{p}$ which are holomorphic on $S_{p}^{\circ}$, continuous on $\partial S_{p}$ and satisfies \begin{equation} \mu_{m}(g)=\sup\limits_{z\in S_{p}}\left|\frac{d^m}{dz}g(z)\right|<\infty,\text{ for all }m\in\mathbb{N}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Even $\tau$-periodic functions on $S_p$, holomorphic inside, with all derivatives bounded.

nodes.name: Seminorms $\mu_m$
nodes.statement: \mu_{m}(g)=\sup\limits_{z\in S_{p}}\left|\frac{d^m}{dz}g(z)\right|<\infty,\text{ for all }m\in\mathbb{N}.
nodes.label: Equation 2.8

nodes.name: $L^2$ isomorphism theorem for the spherical transform (Betori-Faraut-Pagliacci)
nodes.statement: It was proved in \cite{JF} that the spherical Fourier transform is a topological isomorphism from $\mathcal{S}_2(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$ onto $\mathcal{H}(S_{2})^{\#}$.
conclusions: the spherical Fourier transform is a topological isomorphism from $\mathcal{S}_2(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$ onto $\mathcal{H}(S_{2})^{\#}$

nodes.name: $L^p$-tempered distribution
nodes.statement: For $1<p\leq 2$, a linear functional $T:\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})\rightarrow\mathbb{C}$ is said to be a $L^{p}$-tempered distribution if $\langle T,f_{n}\rangle\rightarrow 0$ whenever $\nu_{m}(f_{n})\rightarrow 0$ for all $m\in\mathbb{N}$.

nodes.name: Radial distribution
nodes.statement: The distribution $T$ is said to be radial if $$\langle T,f\rangle=\langle T,\varepsilon f\rangle,\text{ for all }f\in\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X}).$$

nodes.name: Radial part of a distribution
nodes.statement: In fact the radial part of an $L^{p}$-tempered distribution $T$ is again an $L^{p}$-tempered distribution defined by $$\langle\varepsilon T,f\rangle=\langle T,\varepsilon f\rangle,\text{ for all }f\in\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X}).$$

nodes.name: Left translation of a distribution
nodes.statement: The left translation $\tau_{x}$ of $T$ by an element $x\in G$ is defined as follow if $f\in\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})$ then $$\langle \tau_{x}T,f\rangle=T(\tau_{x^{-1}}f)=T\ast f^{\ast}(x^{-1})$$ where $f^{\ast}(x)=f(x^{-1})$.

nodes.name: Spherical Fourier transform of a radial distribution
nodes.statement: Finally, the spherical Fourier transform $\hat{T}$ of a radial $L^{p}$-tempered distribution $T$ is a linear functional on $\mathcal{H}(S_{p})^{\#}$ defined by the following rule: $$\langle \hat{T},\psi\rangle=\langle T,f\rangle,\text{ where }\psi\in\mathcal{H}(S_{p})^{\#}\text{ and }\hat{f}=\psi.$$
nodes.statement_short: $\hat T$ acts on $\mathcal H(S_p)^\#$ by $\langle\hat T,\hat f\rangle=\langle T,f\rangle$.

From the give assumption in Theorem A if we define $T_k=\gamma(z)^{-k}\mathcal L^k f$ then $T_k$ is a $L^2$-tempered distribution and the proof of the Theorem A is a consequence of the Lemma A. It is easy to show that each $T_{k}$ is an $L^p$-tempered distribution which satisfies all the hypothesis of Lemma B1. Hence $\mathcal{L}f=\gamma(i\delta_{p^{\prime}})f$. If $u\in L^{2,\infty}(\mathfrak{X})$ then $f(x)=\int_Ku(x_okx)dk=u(x_o)\phi_z(x)$ also belong to $L^{2,\infty}(\mathfrak{X})$. nodes.name: Fourier transform on $\mathbb{Z}$
nodes.statement: The Fourier transform $\widehat{f}$ of a finitely supported function $f$ defined on $\mathbb{Z}$, is a function on $\mathbb{T}$ given by $$\widehat{f}(s)=\sum\limits_{m\in\mathbb{Z}}f(m)e^{ims}\quad\text{ where }f(m)=\int\limits_{-\pi}^{\pi}\widehat{f}(s)e^{ims}ds$$ represents it's inverse Fourier transform.

nodes.name: Schwartz space $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{Z})$
nodes.statement: Let us define the Schwartz space $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{Z})=\{f:\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}:\lambda_{n}(f)<\infty\text{ for all }n\in\mathbb{N}\}$, equipped with the countable family of semi-norms $\lambda_{n}(f)=\sup(1+|m|)^{n}|f(m)|$.

nodes.name: Fourier isomorphism $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{Z})\to\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb T)$

conclusions: the map $f\rightarrow\widehat{f}$ is a topological isomorphism from $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{Z})$ onto $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb T)$

nodes.name: Distribution on $\mathbb{Z}$ and its Fourier transform
nodes.statement: Analogous to the Euclidean case, a distribution $T$ is a continuous linear functional on $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{Z})$ whose Fourier transform is defined as $$\langle \widehat{T},\phi\rangle=\langle T,\left(\phi^{\vee}\right)^{\#}\rangle,\text{ where }\widehat{\phi^{\vee}}=\phi\text{ and }\left(\phi^{\vee}\right)^{\#}(m)=\phi^{\vee}(-m).$$

Fix $p\in(1,2)$ (proof of the case $p=2$ is similar). Let $f\in\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$ and $z\in S_p$. Then it is clear that the infinite series (ef{eq15}) converges uniformly on $S_p$ and consequently $\hat{f}$ is well-defined. The analyticity of $\hat{f}$ on $S_p^{\circ}$ follows directly from the analyticity of $q^{inz}$ together with the fact that the infinite series (ef{eq15}) converges uniformly on any compact subset of $S_p^{o}$. Infact for every $m\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$, $$\hat{f}^{(m)}(z)=\sum\limits_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}(in\log q)^m\mathcal{A}f(n)q^{inz},\quad	ext{for all } z\in S_p^{o}.$$ The above expression together with equation (ef{eq16}) implies that for every semi-norm $\mu_{m}$ of $\mathcal{H}(S_{p})^{\#}$, there exists a semi-norm $
u_{(m+4)}$ of $\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$ such that, $$\mu_{m}(\hat{f})\leq C
u_{(m+4)}(f)\quad	ext{ for all }f\in\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}.$$ Conversely, assume $g\in\mathcal{H}(S_{p})^{\#}$. Then for all $r$ with $p<r\leq 2$, the function $g(\cdot+i\delta_{r})$ is an infinitely differentiable function of period $	au$. Hence g has a Fourier series representation of the form $g(s)=\sum\limits_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}F(n)q^{ins}$, where $$F(n)= rac{1}{	au}\int\limits_{-	au/2}^{	au/2}g(s)q^{-ins}ds$$ yields the $n^{	ext{th}}$ Fourier co-efficient of the function $g$. Our aim is to prove that $F\in q^{-\delta_{p}|\cdot|}S_{ev}(\mathbb{Z})$. Applying the Cauchy's integral theorem to $g$, it is easy to verify that for every $r\in(p,2]$ and $n\in\mathbb{Z}$,  egin{align} F(n)&= rac{1}{	au}\int\limits_{-	au/2}^{	au/2}g(s+i\delta_{r})q^{-in(s+i\delta_{r})}ds= rac{1}{	au}\int\limits_{-	au/2}^{	au/2}g(s-i\delta_{r})q^{-in(s-i\delta_{r})}ds. \end{align} Infact the first equality in (ef{eq19}) can be proved using the closed rectangle  egin{multline*} \Gamma(z)=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\Im z=0,-	au/2\leq \mbox{Re } z\leq	au/2\}\cup\{z\in\mathbb{C}: \mbox{Re } z=	au/2,0\leq \Im z\leq\delta_{r}\}\ \cup\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\Im z=\delta_{r},	au/2\leq \mbox{Re } z\leq-	au/2\}\cup\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\mbox{Re } z=-	au/2,\delta_{r}\leq \Im z\leq 0\}. \end{multline*} Using the identities (ef{eq19}) and noting that $g$ is even, one can easily prove that $F(-n)=F(n)$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$, that $F$ is even in $\mathbb{Z}$. Integrating by parts the second equation in (ef{eq19}) (m times) and further using the Dominated convergence theorem and letting $rightarrow p$ we have,  egin{equation} \lambda_{m}(q^{\delta_{p}|\cdot|}F)\leq C \mu_{m}(g)\quad	ext{for every }m\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}. \end{equation} Hence there exists an unique $f\in\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$ such that $\mathcal{A}f=F$ and $g=\hat{f}$. Further using equations (ef{eq16}) and (ef{eq21}) we conclude that $$
u_{m}(f)\leq C \mu_{m}(\hat{f})\quad	ext{for every }m\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}.$$ This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Via the Abel transform: bound derivatives of $\hat f$ by Schwartz seminorms; conversely expand $g$ in a Fourier series and shift contours by Cauchy's theorem to get decay of the coefficients.

nodes.name: Contour-shifted Fourier coefficients
nodes.statement: F(n)&=\frac{1}{\tau}\int\limits_{-\tau/2}^{\tau/2}g(s+i\delta_{r})q^{-in(s+i\delta_{r})}ds=\frac{1}{\tau}\int\limits_{-\tau/2}^{\tau/2}g(s-i\delta_{r})q^{-in(s-i\delta_{r})}ds.
nodes.label: eq19

nodes.name: Weighted decay of Fourier coefficients
nodes.statement: \lambda_{m}(q^{\delta_{p}|\cdot|}F)\leq C \mu_{m}(g)\quad\text{for every }m\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}.
nodes.label: eq21

nodes.name: Radial reduction for part (a)
nodes.statement: We first prove part (a) of the theorem with an additional assumption that the distributions $T_{k}$ are radial.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Prove part (a) first for radial distributions.

nodes.name: Write $z_0=\gamma(\alpha)e^{i\theta}$
nodes.statement: Fix $z_{0}\in\mathbb{C}$ such that $|z_{0}|\in[1-b,1+b]$. Then $z_{0}=\gamma(\alpha)e^{i\theta}$ for a unique $\alpha\in[0,\tau/2]$ where $\theta=\arg z_{0}$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Write $z_0=\gamma(\alpha)e^{i\theta}$ with $\alpha\in[0,\tau/2]$.

nodes.name: Fourier relation
nodes.statement: It follows from hypothesis (1) of the theorem that $\mathcal{L}^{k}T_{0}=e^{ik\theta}\gamma(\alpha)^{k}T_{k}$ for every $k\in\mathbb{Z}$. This implies \begin{equation} \widehat{T_{0}}=e^{ik\theta}\left(\frac{\gamma(\alpha)}{\gamma(\cdot)}\right)^{k}\widehat{T_{k}}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Iterate the hypothesis to relate $\widehat{T_0}$ and $\widehat{T_k}$.

nodes.name: Test functions away from $\pm\alpha$
nodes.statement: Let $\phi\in\mathcal{H}(S_{2})^{\#}$ be such that $\mbox{supp}(\phi)\subseteq[-\tau/2,-\alpha-r]\cup[\alpha+r,\tau/2]$ where $r>0$. Observing the fact that $\gamma(\alpha)^{k}/\gamma(\cdot)^{k}\phi\in\mathcal{H}(S_{2})^{\#}$ and using hypothesis (2) of the theorem, we have $$|\langle\widehat{T_{0}},\phi\rangle|=\left|\left\langle\widehat{T_{k}},e^{ik\theta}\left(\frac{\gamma(\alpha)}{\gamma(\cdot)}\right)^{k}\phi\right\rangle\right|=\left|\left\langle T_{k},\left(\left(\frac{\gamma(\alpha)}{\gamma(\cdot)}\right)^{k}\phi\right)^{\vee}\right\rangle\right| \leq M\nu\left[\left(\left(\frac{\gamma(\alpha)}{\gamma(\cdot)}\right)^{k}\phi\right)^{\vee}\right].$$
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Bound $\langle\widehat{T_0},\phi\rangle$ by a seminorm of $(\gamma(\alpha)/\gamma)^k\phi$.

nodes.name: Apply the isomorphism theorem
nodes.statement: By the isomorphism theorem \ref{lp isom}, there exists a fixed seminorm $\mu$ on $\mathcal{H}(S_{2})^{\#}$ such that $$\nu\left[\left(\left(\frac{\gamma(\alpha)}{\gamma(\cdot)}\right)^{k}\phi\right)^{\vee}\right] \leq C\mu\left[\left(\frac{\gamma(\alpha)}{\gamma(\cdot)}\right)^{k}\phi\right]=\sup\limits_{\alpha+r\leq|s|\leq\tau/2}\left|\frac{d^{m}}{ds^{m}}\left(\left(\frac{\gamma(\alpha)}{\gamma(s)}\right)^{k}\phi\right)\right|\rightarrow 0\text{ as }k\rightarrow\infty.$$ By similar argument as above and letting $k\rightarrow -\infty$, we can show that $\langle\widehat{T_{0}},\phi\rangle=0$ for every $\phi\in\mathcal{H}(S_{2})^{\#}$ with $\mbox{supp}(\phi)\subseteq[-\alpha+r,\alpha-r]$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: The isomorphism theorem makes the seminorm tend to $0$ as $k\to\pm\infty$.

nodes.name: Support of $\widehat{T_0}$
nodes.statement: We proved that for any $r>0$ and for every $\phi\in\mathcal{H}(S_{2})^{\#}$ such that $\mbox{supp}(\phi)\subseteq[-\tau/2,-\alpha-r]\cup[-\alpha+r,\alpha-r]\cup[\alpha+r,\tau/2]$, $\langle\widehat{T_{0}},\phi\rangle=0$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: $\widehat{T_0}$ vanishes on test functions supported away from $\pm\alpha$.

nodes.name: Reduce to a Fourier-side identity
nodes.statement: We now show that \begin{equation} (\mathcal{L}-\gamma(\alpha))^{N+1}T_{0}=0\quad\text{for some }N\in\mathbb{Z}_{+} \end{equation} In view of the fact that the spherical transform is an isomorphism from $\mathcal{S}_2(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$ onto $\mathcal{H}(S_{2})^{\#}$, it is enough to prove that \begin{equation} (\gamma(\alpha)-\gamma(s))^{N+1}\widehat{T_{0}}=0\quad\text{for some }N\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Reduce $(\mathcal L-\gamma(\alpha))^{N+1}T_0=0$ to its Fourier-side form.

nodes.name: Cut-off functions $\psi_\epsilon$
nodes.statement: Let $g$ be an infinitely differentiable even function on $\mathbb{R}$ such that $g\equiv 1$ on $[-1/2,1/2]$ and $\mbox{supp}(g)\subseteq(-1,1)$. Define $$\psi_{\epsilon}(s)=\begin{cases} g((s-\alpha)/\epsilon) & s\in[0,\tau/2]\\ g((-s-\alpha)/\epsilon) & s\in[-\tau/2,0]. \end{cases} $$ Here $\epsilon$ is suitably chosen positive number such that $\psi_{\epsilon}\in\mathcal{H}(S_{2})^{\#}$ with $\mbox{supp}(\psi_{\epsilon})\subseteq(-\alpha-\epsilon,-\alpha+\epsilon)\cup(\alpha-\epsilon,\alpha+\epsilon)$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Introduce bump functions $\psi_\epsilon$ concentrated near $\pm\alpha$.

nodes.name: Localize near $\pm\alpha$
nodes.statement:
Note that if $\phi\in\mathcal{H}(S_{2})^{\#}$, then $(\gamma(\alpha)-\gamma(\cdot))^{N+1}\phi(1-\psi_{\epsilon})\in\mathcal{H}(S_{2})^{\#}$ with its support inside $[-	au/2,-\alpha-\epsilon/2]\cup[-\alpha+\epsilon/2,\alpha-\epsilon/2]\cup[\alpha+\epsilon/2,	au/2]$. and using the result proved in step 1, we have  egin{align} |\langle(\gamma(\alpha)-\gamma(s))^{N+1}\widehat{T_{0}},\phiangle| &\leq|\langle\widehat{T_{0}},(\gamma(\alpha)-\gamma(s))^{N+1}\phi(1-\psi_{\epsilon})angle|+|\langle\widehat{T_{0}},(\gamma(\alpha)-\gamma(s))^{N+1}\phi\psi_{\epsilon}angle|
onumber\ &=|\langle\widehat{T_{0}},(\gamma(\alpha)-\gamma(s))^{N+1}\phi\psi_{\epsilon}angle|
onumber\ &\leq M

onumber\ &\leq M\mu\left[(\gamma(\alpha)-\gamma(s))^{N+1}\phi\psi_{\epsilon}ight]
onumber\ &=M\sup\limits_{s\in[-	au/2,	au/2]}\left| rac{d^{m}}{ds^{m}}\left((\gamma(\alpha)-\gamma(s))^{N+1}\phi(s)\psi_{\epsilon}(s)ight)ight|
onumber\ &=M\sup\limits_{\alpha-\epsilon\leq |s|\leq\alpha+\epsilon}\left| rac{d^{m}}{ds^{m}}\left((\gamma(\alpha)-\gamma(s))^{N+1}\phi(s)\psi_{\epsilon}(s)ight)ight|
onumber\ &\leq M\sum\limits_{i=0}^{m} inom{m}{i}\sup\limits_{\alpha-\epsilon\leq |s|\leq\alpha+\epsilon}\left| rac{d^{i}}{ds^{i}}\left((\gamma(\alpha)-\gamma(s))^{N+1}ight)ight|
onumber\ &\hspace*{5cm}	imes\sup\limits_{\alpha-\epsilon\leq |s|\leq\alpha+\epsilon}\left| rac{d^{m-i}}{ds^{m-i}}\left(\phi(s)\psi_{\epsilon}(s)ight)ight|. \end{align}
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Split $\phi$ with $\psi_\epsilon$ and bound the remaining term by Leibniz.

nodes.name: Derivative estimates
nodes.statement: Choose $N$ large enough e.g. $N=10m+1$. Then for every $s\in(\alpha-\epsilon,\alpha+\epsilon)$ we have the following estimates: \begin{enumerate} \item[(i)] $\left|\frac{d^{i}}{ds^{i}}\left((\gamma(\alpha)-\gamma(s))^{10m+2}\right)\right|\leq B_{m}|\gamma(\alpha)-\gamma(s)|^{10m+2-i}$ where $0\leq i\leq m$ and \item [(ii)] $\left|\frac{d^{m-i}}{ds^{m-i}}\left(\phi(s)\psi_{\epsilon}(s)\right)\right|\leq C_{m,\phi}/\epsilon^{m-i}.$ \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Take $N=10m+1$ and estimate the two derivative factors.

nodes.name: Let $\epsilon\to0$
nodes.statement: The above estimates together with (\ref{eq26}) implies that \begin{align*} \mu\left[(\gamma(\alpha)-\gamma(s))^{N+1}\phi\psi_{\epsilon}\right]&\leq M_{m,\phi}\sum\limits_{i=0}^{m}\sup\limits_{\alpha-\epsilon\leq |s|\leq\alpha+\epsilon}|\gamma(\alpha)-\gamma(s)|^{10m+2-i}\frac{1}{\epsilon^{m-i}}\\ &\leq D\epsilon^{9m+2}\rightarrow 0\text{ as }\epsilon\rightarrow 0. \end{align*} This proves (\ref{eq25}).
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: The seminorm is $O(\epsilon^{9m+2})\to0$, proving (11).

nodes.name: Reduce to $N=0$
nodes.statement: Using the same argument given in \cite{KRS2} one can easily prove that $$(\mathcal{L}-\gamma(\alpha))T_{0}=0.$$ This prove part (a) for radial distribution.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: As in [KRS2], get $(\mathcal L-\gamma(\alpha))T_0=0$ for radial $T_k$.

nodes.name: General case setup
nodes.statement: Now we shall prove the result for general case. To avoid triviality, we further assume that $T_{k}$ is nonzero for some (and hence for all) $k\in\mathbb{Z}$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Turn to non-radial $T_k$, assumed nonzero.

nodes.name: Radial parts of translates detect $T$
nodes.statement: Observe that for any $L^{2}$-tempered distribution $T$, if $\varepsilon(\tau_{x}T)=0$ for every $x\in\mathfrak{X}$ then $T=0$. Indeed the above assumption on $T$ implies that $$\langle\tau_{x}T,\delta_{0}\rangle=T\ast\delta_{0}(x^{-1})=0$$ for all $x\in\mathfrak{X}$, where $\delta_{0}$ denotes the Dirac-Delta function at $o$. Since $T\ast\delta_{0}=T$ in the sense of distribution thus $T=0$. This shows that for every $k\in\mathbb{Z}$, there exists an $x\in\mathfrak{X}$ such that the distribution $\tau_{x}T_{k}$ has a nonzero radial part.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: A distribution all of whose translates have zero radial part is zero.

nodes.name: Claim: nonvanishing propagates in $k$
nodes.statement:
Now we claim that if $\varepsilon(	au_{x}T_{0})
eq 0$ for some $x\in\mathfrak{X}$, then $\varepsilon(	au_{x}T_{k})
eq 0$ for every $k\in\mathbb{Z}$. To prove this it is enough to show that if $\varepsilon(	au_{x}T_{0})
eq 0$ for some $x\in\mathfrak{X}$, then $\varepsilon(	au_{x}T_{-1})
eq 0$ and $\varepsilon(	au_{x}T_{1})
eq 0$. If $\varepsilon(	au_{x}T_{-1})=0$ then $\mathcal{L}\varepsilon(	au_{x}T_{-1})=0$. Since $\mathcal L$ commutes with translation and radialization, and $\mathcal{L}T_{-1}=z_0T_{0}$ for $z_0
eq 0$ thus $\varepsilon(	au_{x}T_{0})=0$. On the other hand if $\varepsilon(	au_{x}T_{1})=0$ then $$\langle	au_{x}T_{1},\phiangle=\langle	au_{x}\mathcal{L}T_{0},\phiangle=\langle	au_{x}T_{0},\mathcal{L}\phiangle=0$$ for every $\phi\in\mathcal{S}_2(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$. Since $\gamma(s)^{-1}\hat{\psi}(s)\in\mathcal{H}(S_{2})^{\#}$ for every $\psi\in\mathcal{S}_2(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$. Thus $\psi$ can be written as $\psi=\mathcal{L}\phi$ for some $\phi\in\mathcal{S}_2(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$. Hence $	au_{x}T_{0}=0$ for all $x\in\mathfrak X$. This proves our claim.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Nonzero radial part of $\tau_xT_0$ forces nonzero radial parts for all $k$.

nodes.name: Reduce to neighbours
nodes.statement:
To prove this it is enough to show that if $\varepsilon(	au_{x}T_{0})
eq 0$ for some $x\in\mathfrak{X}$, then $\varepsilon(	au_{x}T_{-1})
eq 0$ and $\varepsilon(	au_{x}T_{1})
eq 0$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Suffices to treat $k=\pm1$.

nodes.name: Case $k=-1$
nodes.statement: If $\varepsilon(\tau_{x}T_{-1})=0$ then $\mathcal{L}\varepsilon(\tau_{x}T_{-1})=0$. Since $\mathcal L$ commutes with translation and radialization, and $\mathcal{L}T_{-1}=z_0T_{0}$ for $z_0\neq 0$ thus $\varepsilon(\tau_{x}T_{0})=0$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Use that $\mathcal L$ commutes with translation and radialization.

nodes.name: Case $k=1$
nodes.statement: On the other hand if $\varepsilon(\tau_{x}T_{1})=0$ then $$\langle\tau_{x}T_{1},\phi\rangle=\langle\tau_{x}\mathcal{L}T_{0},\phi\rangle=\langle\tau_{x}T_{0},\mathcal{L}\phi\rangle=0$$ for every $\phi\in\mathcal{S}_2(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$. Since $\gamma(s)^{-1}\hat{\psi}(s)\in\mathcal{H}(S_{2})^{\#}$ for every $\psi\in\mathcal{S}_2(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$. Thus $\psi$ can be written as $\psi=\mathcal{L}\phi$ for some $\phi\in\mathcal{S}_2(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$. Hence $\tau_{x}T_{0}=0$ for all $x\in\mathfrak X$. This proves our claim.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Invert $\mathcal L$ on radial Schwartz functions to conclude $\tau_xT_0=0$.

nodes.name: Apply the radial case
nodes.statement: It is easy to show that for every $x\in\mathfrak{X}$, the sequence $\{\varepsilon(\tau_{x}T_{k})\}$ of radial distributions satisfies the hypothesis of this theorem. Since the result is already proved for radial $L^{2}$-tempered distributions, we have $$\mathcal{L}\varepsilon(\tau_{x}T_{0})=|z|\varepsilon(\tau_{x}T_{0})\quad\text{for all }x\in\mathfrak{X}.$$ Therefore $\varepsilon(\tau_{x}(\mathcal{L}T_{0}-|z|T_{0}))=0$ for all $x\in\mathfrak{X}$. From above observation we have $\mathcal{L}T_{0}=|z|T_{0}$. This complete the proof of part (a).
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Apply the radial result to $\varepsilon(\tau_xT_k)$ and conclude part (a).

nodes.name: Part (b) estimate
nodes.statement: We shall prove part (b) of the theorem only for radial case. The proof for the general case follows in a similar way as in part (a). Now assuming that $T_{k}$ are radial, we have for any $\phi\in\mathcal{S}_2(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$, $$ |\langle\widehat{T_{0}},\phi\rangle|=\left|\left\langle\widehat{T_{k}},\left(\frac{z_{0}}{\gamma(s)}\right)^{k}\phi\right\rangle\right| \leq M\nu\left[\left(\left(\frac{z_{0}}{\gamma(s)}\right)^{k}\phi\right)^{\vee}\right] \leq M\mu\left[\left(\frac{z_{0}}{\gamma(s)}\right)^{k}\phi\right].$$
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Bound $\langle\widehat{T_0},\phi\rangle$ by $\mu[(z_0/\gamma)^k\phi]$.

nodes.name: Conclude part (b)
nodes.statement: If $|z_{0}|<\gamma(s)$ (resp. $|z_{0}|>\gamma(s)$) for $s\in[-\tau/2,\tau/2]$, then letting $k\rightarrow\infty$ (resp. $k\rightarrow -\infty$) in the above equation we conclude that $\langle T_{0},\phi\rangle=0$ for all $\phi\in\mathcal{S}_2(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$. This completes the proof.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Let $k\to\pm\infty$ to get $T_0=0$.

nodes.name: Radial reduction
nodes.statement: We prove the this result for radial distributions, while the general case follows in a similar way as in Theorem \ref{Theorem10}.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Treat radial distributions; the general case is as in Lemma A.

nodes.name: Claim: Fourier-side finite-order relation
nodes.statement: For $p\in(1,2)$ let $z_{0}=i\delta_{p^{\prime}}$. For a fixed $N\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$ we claim that $$(\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\widehat{T_{0}}=0.$$ As observed earlier, for any $\phi\in\mathcal{H}(S_{p})^{\#}$ we have, $$ |\langle(\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\widehat{T_{0}},\phi\rangle|\leq M\mu\left[\left(\left(\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right)^{k}(\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\phi\right)\right].$$ Since $\gamma(z)$ and $\phi(z)$ are $\tau-$periodic, even functions on $S_{p}$, so the seminorm $\mu$ on $\mathcal{H}(S_{p})^{\#}$ is given by \begin{align*} \mu\left[\left(\left(\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right)^{k}(\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\phi\right)\right]&=\sup\limits_{z\in S_{p}}\left|\frac{d^{m}}{dz^{m}}\left(\left(\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right)^{k}(\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\phi(z)\right)\right|\\ &=\sup\limits_{z\in S_{p}^{+}}\left|\frac{d^{m}}{dz^{m}}\left(\left(\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right)^{k}(\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\phi(z)\right)\right|\\ &=\sup\limits_{z\in S_{p}^{+}} F_{k}(z)\text{ (say),} \end{align*} where $S_{p}^{+}=\{z\in S_{p}:~\; |\mbox{Re } z|\leq \tau/2\;\; \text{and}\;\; \Im z\geq 0\}$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Claim $(\gamma(z_0)-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\widehat{T_0}=0$ and express the seminorm as $\sup F_k$.

nodes.name: Seminorm bound
nodes.statement: As observed earlier, for any $\phi\in\mathcal{H}(S_{p})^{\#}$ we have, $$ |\langle(\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\widehat{T_{0}},\phi\rangle|\leq M\mu\left[\left(\left(\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right)^{k}(\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\phi\right)\right].$$
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Bound the pairing by $\mu$ of $(\gamma(z_0)/\gamma)^k(\gamma(z_0)-\gamma)^{N+1}\phi$.

nodes.name: Reduce to $S_p^+$
nodes.statement: Since $\gamma(z)$ and $\phi(z)$ are $\tau-$periodic, even functions on $S_{p}$, so the seminorm $\mu$ on $\mathcal{H}(S_{p})^{\#}$ is given by \begin{align*} \mu\left[\left(\left(\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right)^{k}(\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\phi\right)\right]&=\sup\limits_{z\in S_{p}}\left|\frac{d^{m}}{dz^{m}}\left(\left(\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right)^{k}(\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\phi(z)\right)\right|\\ &=\sup\limits_{z\in S_{p}^{+}}\left|\frac{d^{m}}{dz^{m}}\left(\left(\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right)^{k}(\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\phi(z)\right)\right|\\ &=\sup\limits_{z\in S_{p}^{+}} F_{k}(z)\text{ (say),} \end{align*} where $S_{p}^{+}=\{z\in S_{p}:~\; |\mbox{Re } z|\leq \tau/2\;\; \text{and}\;\; \Im z\geq 0\}$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: By symmetry the supremum can be taken over $S_p^+$.

nodes.name: Reduce to $\sup F_k\to0$
nodes.statement: To prove our claim it is enough to show that $\sup\limits_{z\in S_{p}^{+}} F_{k}\rightarrow 0$ as $k\rightarrow\infty$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Suffices to show $\sup_{S_p^+}F_k\to0$.

nodes.name: Leibniz bound on $F_k$
nodes.statement: Now for all $z\in S_{p}^{+}$, \begin{align} F_{k}(z)&\leq\sum\limits_{i=0}^{m}\binom{m}{i}\left|\frac{d^{i}}{dz^{i}}\left(\left(\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right)^{k}\right)\right| \left|\frac{d^{m-i}}{dz^{m-i}}\left((\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\phi(z)\right)\right|\nonumber\\ &\leq\sum\limits_{i=0}^{m}\binom{m}{i}B_{m}\left|\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right|^{k}k(k+1)(k+2)\ldots(k+i-1) \\ &\hspace*{4.8cm}\times\left|\frac{d^{m-i}}{dz^{m-i}}\left((\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\phi(z)\right)\right|.\nonumber \end{align} From above inequality we also have \begin{equation}F_{k}(z)\leq A_{m}k^{m}\left|\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right|^{k} \end{equation} where $A_{m}=\max\limits_{0\leq i\leq m}\left[\sup\limits_{z\in S_{p}^{+}}\left|\frac{d^{i}}{dz^{i}}\left((\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\phi(z)\right)\right|\right].$
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Leibniz rule gives $F_k\le A_mk^m|\gamma(z_0)/\gamma(z)|^k$.

nodes.name: Auxiliary estimates
nodes.statement: In the above calculation we have also used the following estimates. For every $z\in S_{p}^{+}$, \begin{enumerate} \item[(i)] $\left|\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right|\leq 1$, \item[(ii)] $\left|\frac{d^{i}}{dz^{i}}\left(\left(\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right)^{k}\right)\right|\leq B_{m}\left|\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right|^{k}k(k+1)(k+2)\ldots(k+i-1)$, where $0\leq i\leq m$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Record $|\gamma(z_0)/\gamma(z)|\le1$ and derivative bounds.

nodes.name: Split into $V_k$ and $V_k^c$
nodes.statement: In order to prove that $\sup\limits_{z\in S_{p}^{+}} F_{k}\rightarrow 0$ as $k\rightarrow\infty$, it is enough to show that \begin{enumerate} \item[(a)] $\sup\limits_{z\in V_{k}^{c}} F_{k}\rightarrow 0$, \item[(b)] $\sup\limits_{z\in V_{k}} F_{k}\rightarrow 0$ as $k\rightarrow\infty$. \end{enumerate} where for $k$ (large enough) $$V_{k}=\{z\in S_{p}^{+}: |\mbox{Re } z|<(k^{1/4}\log q)^{-1}\text{ and } \delta_{p}-\log(1+1/k^{1/6})(\log q)^{-1}<\Im z\leq\delta_{p}\}.$$
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Split $S_p^+$ into a shrinking neighbourhood $V_k$ of $z_0$ and its complement.

nodes.name: Target estimate on $V_k^c$
nodes.statement: First we deal with (a). In view of equation (\ref{eq31}), it is sufficient to show that for every $z\in V_{k}^{c}$ there exists a constant $c>0$ such that \begin{equation} \left|\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right|^{k}\leq\left(1+\frac{c}{\sqrt{k}}\right)^{-k}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: On $V_k^c$ it suffices to show $|\gamma(z_0)/\gamma(z)|^k\le(1+c/\sqrt k)^{-k}$.

nodes.name: Case: small imaginary part
nodes.statement: First case, if $0\leq \Im z\leq \delta_{p}-\frac{\log(1+1/k^{1/6})}{\log q}$ then $|\gamma(z)|\geq |\gamma(i(\delta_{p}-\frac{\log(1+1/k^{1/6})}{\log q}))|$. Hence \begin{align} |\gamma(z)|-|\gamma(z_{0})|&\geq \left(\frac{q^{1/p}+q^{1/p^{\prime}}}{q+1}\right)-\left(\frac{q^{1/p}(1+k^{-1/6})^{-1}+q^{1/p^{\prime}}(1+k^{-1/6})}{q+1}\right)\nonumber\\ &=\frac{1}{q+1}\frac{q^{1/p^{\prime}}}{k^{1/6}(1+k^{1/6})}\left[k^{1/6}(q^{2/p-1}-1)-1\right]. \end{align} Since $q^{2/p-1}-1>0$, there exists $k_{0}\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $k^{1/6}(q^{2/p-1}-1)\geq 2$ for every $k\geq k_{0}$. This together with (\ref{eq33}) gives the desired inequality (\ref{eq32}).
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Lower-bound $|\gamma(z)|-|\gamma(z_0)|$ when $\Im z$ is away from $\delta_p$.

nodes.name: Case: large real part
nodes.statement: Other case if $z\in V_{k}^{c}$ is such that $\tau/2\geq|\mbox{Re } z|\geq (k^{1/4}\log q)^{-1}$, then $$|\gamma(z)|\geq \left(1-\frac{q^{1/p^{\prime}}+q^{1/p}}{q+1}cos(k^{-1/4})\right)$$ and $$|\gamma(z)|-|\gamma(z_{0})|\geq\left(\frac{q^{1/p^{\prime}}+q^{1/p}}{q+1}(1-\cos(k^{-1/4}))\right)\geq \frac{c}{k^{1/2}}.$$
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Lower-bound $|\gamma(z)|-|\gamma(z_0)|$ when $|\Re z|\ge(k^{1/4}\log q)^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Conclude on $V_k^c$
nodes.statement: Thus for every $z\in V_{k}^{c}$, inequality (\ref{eq32}) holds. Eventually, $\sup\limits_{z\in V_{k}^{c}} F_{k}\rightarrow 0$ as $k\rightarrow\infty$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Hence $\sup_{V_k^c}F_k\to0$.

nodes.name: Estimate on $V_k$
nodes.statement: Now let us assume that $z\in V_{k}$. Then $z=a+i\delta_{r}$, where $|a|<(k^{1/4}\log q)^{-1}$ and $\delta_{p}-\log(1+1/k^{1/6})(\log q)^{-1}<\delta_{r}\leq\delta_{p}$ and we have \begin{align*} |\gamma(z)-\gamma(z_{0})|^{2}&=\left(\frac{q^{1/p^{\prime}}+q^{1/p}}{q+1}-\frac{q^{1/r^{\prime}}+q^{1/r}}{q+1}\cos(a\log q)\right)^{2} +\left(\frac{q^{1/r}-q^{1/r^{\prime}}}{q+1}\right)^{2}\sin^{2}(a\log q)\\ &\leq \left(\frac{q^{1/p}+q^{1/p^{\prime}}}{q+1}-\frac{q^{1/p}(1+k^{-1/6})^{-1}+q^{1/p^{\prime}}(1+k^{-1/6})}{q+1}\cos(k^{-1/4})\right)^{2}\\ &\hspace*{8cm}+\left(\frac{q^{1/p}-q^{1/p^{\prime}}}{q+1}\right)^{2}\sin^{2}(k^{-1/4}) \end{align*} It follows from the inequality $\sqrt{|x|^2+|y|^2}\leq |x|+|y|$ that \begin{align*} |\gamma(z)-\gamma(z_{0})|&\leq \left(\frac{q^{1/p}+q^{1/p^{\prime}}}{q+1}-\frac{q^{1/p}(1+k^{-1/6})^{-1}+q^{1/p^{\prime}}(1+k^{-1/6})}{q+1}\cos(k^{-1/4})\right)+\frac{c_{1}}{k^{1/4}}\\ &= \left(\frac{q^{1/p}+q^{1/p^{\prime}}}{q+1}-\frac{q^{1/p}(1+k^{-1/6})^{-1}+q^{1/p^{\prime}}(1+k^{-1/6})}{q+1}\right)\\ &\hspace*{3cm}+\frac{q^{1/p}(1+k^{-1/6})^{-1}+q^{1/p^{\prime}}(1+k^{-1/6})}{q+1}(1-\cos(k^{-1/4}))+\frac{c_{1}}{k^{1/4}}\\ &\leq \frac{c_{3}}{k^{1/6}}+\frac{c_{2}}{k^{1/2}}+\frac{c_{1}}{k^{1/4}}\leq\frac{c}{k^{1/6}}, \end{align*} where the constants $c_{1},c_{2},c_{3}$ (and hence $c$) are independent of $k$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: On $V_k$, $|\gamma(z)-\gamma(z_0)|\le c/k^{1/6}$.

nodes.name: Conclude $\sup F_k\to0$
nodes.statement: If we take $N=7m+1$ then each term in equation (\ref{eq30}) atleast contains the factor $(\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1-m}=(\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{6m+2}$. Thus from above estimates and equation (\ref{eq30}), we finally have $\sup\limits_{z\in V_{k}} F_{k}\leq \frac{C}{k^{1/3}},$ where $C$ is independent of $k$ and $\sup\limits_{z\in S_{p}} F_{k}\rightarrow 0$ as $k\rightarrow\infty$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: With $N=7m+1$ the factor $(\gamma(z_0)-\gamma)^{6m+2}$ gives $\sup_{V_k}F_k\le C/k^{1/3}$.

nodes.name: Reduce to $N=0$
nodes.statement: Using the same argument given in \cite{KRS2} one can easily prove that $N=0$. This completes the proof of part (a) for radial and eventually for general distributions.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: As in [KRS2], $N=0$, proving part (a).

nodes.name: Part (b)
nodes.statement: The proof of part (b) is similar to that of part (b) Lemma A.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Part (b) as in Lemma A.

nodes.name: Part (c) setup
nodes.statement: To prove part (c), assume that $\gamma(\tau/2+i\delta_{p^{\prime}})>|\lambda|>\gamma(i\delta_{p^{\prime}})$. Then $\gamma(S_{p}^{\circ})$ intersects $\{w\in\mathbb C:|w|=|\lambda|\}$ at infinitely many points.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: In the intermediate range the circle $|w|=|\lambda|$ meets $\gamma(S_p^\circ)$ infinitely often.

nodes.name: Counterexample for part (c)
nodes.statement: Let $p<q<r<2$ be such that $\gamma(\alpha+i\delta_{q^{\prime}})e^{-i\theta_1}=\gamma(\beta+i\delta_{r^{\prime}})e^{-i\theta_2}=\lambda$ for some $\theta_1,\theta_2\in(0,2\pi)$. If we define $T_{k}=e^{ik\theta_1}\phi_{\alpha+i\delta_{q^{\prime}}}+e^{ik\theta_2}\phi_{\beta+i\delta_{r^{\prime}}}$ where $k\in\mathbb Z_{+}$, then $T_k$ satisfies all the hypothesis of Lemma B1 but $T_0$ fails to be an eigen-distribution of $\mathcal L$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: A sum of two spherical functions satisfies the hypotheses but is not an eigen-distribution.

nodes.name: Theorem A from Lemma A
nodes.statement: \noindent {\it Proof of Theorem A and Theorem B:} Now we will conclude the rest of the proof of the our main theorems. Let $z_0=\gamma(z)$ for $z\in\mathbb R\setminus\tau/2\mathbb Z$. From the give assumption in Theorem A if we define $T_k=\gamma(z)^{-k}\mathcal L^k f$ then $T_k$ is a $L^2$-tempered distribution and the proof of the Theorem A is a consequence of the Lemma A.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Set $T_k=\gamma(z)^{-k}\mathcal L^kf$ and apply Lemma A.

nodes.name: Theorem B part 1 from Lemma B1
nodes.statement: Similarly if we assume that $T_{k}=\gamma(i\delta_{p^{\prime}})^{-k}\mathcal{L}^{k}f$ where $k\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$. According to the hypothesis of Theorem B, $\|T_{k}\|_{p^\prime,\infty}\leq M$ for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$. It is easy to show that each $T_{k}$ is an $L^p$-tempered distribution which satisfies all the hypothesis of Lemma B1. Hence $\mathcal{L}f=\gamma(i\delta_{p^{\prime}})f$. This completes the proof of the 1st part of Theorem B.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Set $T_k=\gamma(i\delta_{p'})^{-k}\mathcal L^kf$ and apply Lemma B1.

nodes.name: Theorem B part 2 from Lemma B2
nodes.statement: The remaining part of Theorem B will follow from the Lemma B2.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Part 2 of Theorem B follows from Lemma B2.

nodes.name: Radialize $u$
nodes.statement: Assume $u(x_o)\neq 0$ for some $x_o\in \mathfrak X$. If $u\in L^{2,\infty}(\mathfrak{X})$ then $f(x)=\int_Ku(x_okx)dk=u(x_o)\phi_z(x)$ also belong to $L^{2,\infty}(\mathfrak{X})$.
nodes.section: 4 Sharpness of the main results and the case $q=1$
nodes.statement_short: If $u$ were weak-$L^2$, so would be its radialization $u(x_o)\phi_z$.

nodes.name: Contradiction via Lemma 2.1
nodes.statement: In view of Lemma \ref{phiz} this not true as $\phi_{z}$ does not belong to $L^{2,\infty}(\mathfrak{X})$ whenever $z\in(\tau/2)\mathbb{Z}$.
nodes.section: 4 Sharpness of the main results and the case $q=1$
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 2.1 says $\phi_z\notin L^{2,\infty}$ for these $z$.

nodes.name: Fix $p$, $f$, $z$
nodes.statement: Fix $p\in(1,2)$ (proof of the case $p=2$ is similar). Let $f\in\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$ and $z\in S_p$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix $p\in(1,2)$, $f\in\mathcal S_p^\#$ and $z\in S_p$.

nodes.name: $\hat f$ is well defined and holomorphic
nodes.statement: Then it is clear that the infinite series (\ref{eq15}) converges uniformly on $S_p$ and consequently $\hat{f}$ is well-defined. The analyticity of $\hat{f}$ on $S_p^{\circ}$ follows directly from the analyticity of $q^{inz}$ together with the fact that the infinite series (\ref{eq15}) converges uniformly on any compact subset of $S_p^{o}$. Infact for every $m\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$, $$\hat{f}^{(m)}(z)=\sum\limits_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}(in\log q)^m\mathcal{A}f(n)q^{inz},\quad\text{for all } z\in S_p^{o}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Uniform convergence of the Abel series gives holomorphy and a derivative formula.

nodes.name: Forward continuity
nodes.statement: The above expression together with equation (\ref{eq16}) implies that for every semi-norm $\mu_{m}$ of $\mathcal{H}(S_{p})^{\#}$, there exists a semi-norm $\nu_{(m+4)}$ of $\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$ such that, $$\mu_{m}(\hat{f})\leq C\nu_{(m+4)}(f)\quad\text{ for all }f\in\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Bound $\mu_m(\hat f)$ by $\nu_{m+4}(f)$.

nodes.name: Fourier series of $g$
nodes.statement: Conversely, assume $g\in\mathcal{H}(S_{p})^{\#}$. Then for all $r$ with $p<r\leq 2$, the function $g(\cdot+i\delta_{r})$ is an infinitely differentiable function of period $\tau$. Hence g has a Fourier series representation of the form $g(s)=\sum\limits_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}F(n)q^{ins}$, where $$F(n)=\frac{1}{\tau}\int\limits_{-\tau/2}^{\tau/2}g(s)q^{-ins}ds$$ yields the $n^{\text{th}}$ Fourier co-efficient of the function $g$.
nodes.statement_short: Expand $g\in\mathcal H(S_p)^\#$ in a Fourier series with coefficients $F(n)$.

nodes.name: Contour shift
nodes.statement: Our aim is to prove that $F\in q^{-\delta_{p}|\cdot|}S_{ev}(\mathbb{Z})$. Applying the Cauchy's integral theorem to $g$, it is easy to verify that for every $r\in(p,2]$ and $n\in\mathbb{Z}$, \begin{align} F(n)&=\frac{1}{\tau}\int\limits_{-\tau/2}^{\tau/2}g(s+i\delta_{r})q^{-in(s+i\delta_{r})}ds=\frac{1}{\tau}\int\limits_{-\tau/2}^{\tau/2}g(s-i\delta_{r})q^{-in(s-i\delta_{r})}ds. \end{align} Infact the first equality in (\ref{eq19}) can be proved using the closed rectangle \begin{multline*} \Gamma(z)=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\Im z=0,-\tau/2\leq \mbox{Re } z\leq\tau/2\}\cup\{z\in\mathbb{C}: \mbox{Re } z=\tau/2,0\leq \Im z\leq\delta_{r}\}\\ \cup\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\Im z=\delta_{r},\tau/2\leq \mbox{Re } z\leq-\tau/2\}\cup\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\mbox{Re } z=-\tau/2,\delta_{r}\leq \Im z\leq 0\}. \end{multline*}
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy's theorem shifts the coefficient integral to $\Im s=\pm\delta_r$.

nodes.name: $F$ is even
nodes.statement: Using the identities (\ref{eq19}) and noting that $g$ is even, one can easily prove that $F(-n)=F(n)$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$, that $F$ is even in $\mathbb{Z}$.
nodes.statement_short: Evenness of $g$ gives $F(-n)=F(n)$.

nodes.name: Weighted decay of $F$
nodes.statement: Integrating by parts the second equation in (\ref{eq19}) (m times) and further using the Dominated convergence theorem and letting $r\rightarrow p$ we have, \begin{equation} \lambda_{m}(q^{\delta_{p}|\cdot|}F)\leq C \mu_{m}(g)\quad\text{for every }m\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Integration by parts and $r\to p$ give $\lambda_m(q^{\delta_p|\cdot|}F)\le C\mu_m(g)$.

nodes.name: Inverse and its continuity
nodes.statement: Hence there exists an unique $f\in\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$ such that $\mathcal{A}f=F$ and $g=\hat{f}$. Further using equations (\ref{eq16}) and (\ref{eq21}) we conclude that $$\nu_{m}(f)\leq C \mu_{m}(\hat{f})\quad\text{for every }m\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}.$$ This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: The Abel isomorphism yields $f$ with $\hat f=g$ and $\nu_m(f)\le C\mu_m(\hat f)$.
